standard.text: How does pressing a tiny cap turn calm perfume at the bottom of a bottle into a floating mist cloud? Inside the neck sits a tiny hand pump with a spring, two one-way seals, and a pinhole just three tenths of a millimeter wide. Let's watch what happens from the very first press.
Start with a brand-new fifty milliliter bottle. The golden perfume fills the glass base, but the long straw and the small pump chamber above it start completely full of air.
Now press the orange spray cap down for the first time. Inside the pump chamber, the piston compresses the spring and pushes the trapped air out through the tip.

Let go, and the spring pushes the cap back up. That creates gentle suction in the pump chamber, lifting the tiny bottom ball and pulling golden perfume right up the straw. It takes two priming presses to fill this bottle's straw and chamber.

Now the chamber is primed with perfume. Press the orange cap again: the bottom ball seals shut so liquid cannot go back down, and the squeezed perfume shoots through the tiny pinhole, shattering into a fine mist cloud reaching twenty-five centimeters.
Let go once more. A one-way seal at the nozzle blocks outside air from sneaking in, so the rising spring pulls a fresh dose up the straw to refill the pump chamber for your next spray.

Finally, when the perfume level drops below five percent, the bottom tip of the straw pokes out into air. The pump pulls air instead of liquid and only sputters, until you tilt the bottle so the straw reaches the last drops.
